x.A: A WAF web ACL can block traffic by rules, but it doesn't give a DDoS audit trail or mitigation support from AWS experts, and blocking unknown random IP addresses isn't practical.
x.B: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities and has nothing to do with DDoS protection, and the DDoS Response Team works with Shield Advanced customers.
x.C: Shield Advanced protects the ALB against DDoS attacks with minimal configuration, gives visibility into attack sources and an audit trail, and lets you engage the DDoS Response Team.
x.D: CloudFront with WAF adds changes to the architecture, which the city wants to minimize, and it doesn't give DDoS source auditing the way Shield Advanced does.

x.A: A file gateway adds caching and a gateway layer, so it doesn't give consistent sub-millisecond latency and high throughput for an HPC cluster.
x.B: Importing the data into S3 and linking it to FSx for Lustre gives the HPC cluster sub-millisecond latency and high throughput through a Lustre file system that loads the S3 data.
x.C: EFS has higher latency than Lustre and copying data from S3 to EFS is extra work, and it doesn't give sub-millisecond latency.
x.D: Snowball Edge devices import data into S3, not directly into an FSx for Lustre file system.

x.A: Glue is an ETL service and isn't used to copy NFS data to S3.
x.B: A DataSync agent on premises copies data from NFS servers to S3 on a schedule, and you pay per GB copied. For small amounts of data it's the lowest cost with little setup.
x.C: Transfer for SFTP has hourly endpoint charges and requires SFTP changes, so it costs more and doesn't read from NFS directly.
x.D: A Direct Connect connection is expensive and slow to set up for small periodic backups.

x.A: An ALB handles HTTP and HTTPS, so it can't carry UDP traffic.
x.B: A Gateway Load Balancer is for inserting virtual appliances into the traffic path, not for distributing game traffic to servers.
x.C: An NLB handles millions of UDP requests per second with ultra-low latency, and it costs less than the alternatives for this workload.
x.D: Running identical servers in several Regions adds cost and doesn't handle the UDP load by itself.

x.A: DMS Schema Conversion transforms the MySQL schema and database objects into the PostgreSQL format, which is needed when changing engines.
x.B: Schema Conversion can't create a read replica. A read replica can't be created across different engines.
x.C: An Aurora MySQL read replica would keep the engine as MySQL, but the target is Aurora PostgreSQL.
x.D: A DMS task with change data capture (CDC) replicates the changes that happen during the migration to the new database.
x.E: Aurora PostgreSQL can't be a replica of a MySQL database, so there is no replica to promote.

x.A: A script that picks the instance with the fewest connections doesn't help, because a Multi-AZ standby can't be queried and the primary is the only readable instance.
x.B: A read replica receives copies of the data, and pointing the reporting script to it moves the load off the primary database. It needs little operational effort.
x.C: Manual daily exports are manual work and don't solve the performance problem during the day.
x.D: A cache doesn't help a script that reports new entries, because it needs fresh data.

x.A: CloudTrail records API calls to AWS services and doesn't show the traffic requests to the ALB.
x.B: ALB access logs, delivered to S3, record each request, and Athena queries them with SQL without any servers, so it's the most efficient way to analyze the traffic.
x.C: Opening log files one by one in a text editor is manual and doesn't scale.
x.D: EMR on a dedicated EC2 instance can't query the ALB directly, and it adds overhead.

x.A: A public NAT gateway must be in a public subnet to reach the internet gateway, so placing it in a private subnet doesn't work.
x.B: A private NAT gateway doesn't provide internet access. It's for connecting to other VPCs or on-premises networks.
x.C: A public NAT gateway in a public subnet has a route to the internet gateway, and the private subnets send internet-bound traffic through it.
x.D: A private NAT gateway can't connect to the public internet, even in a public subnet.

x.A: Attaching the SCP to the root OU applies it to all accounts, including the production account, which must be able to launch those instances.
x.B: Attaching the SCP directly to the three nonproduction accounts applies it only to them.
x.C: The management account isn't affected by SCPs, so attaching to it does nothing.
x.D: Attaching the SCP to an OU for the production account blocks the production account, which is the opposite of the requirement.
x.E: Creating an OU for the nonproduction accounts, attaching the SCP to it, and moving those accounts into it restricts only them.

x.A: A VPC endpoint for S3 gives a private connection between EC2 and S3, and a bucket policy that allows access only from the endpoint makes the connection private and secure.
x.B: An IAM policy gives permission but doesn't make the connection private, because the traffic could still use the internet.
x.C: A NAT gateway sends traffic out to the internet, so it isn't private.
x.D: Access keys are credentials, not a private network path, and long-term keys are insecure.

x.A: Logging state changes with EventBridge and Lambda doesn't add capacity for reads or writes.
x.B: Zero-downtime restart helps with maintenance restarts, and Database Activity Streams is for auditing, so neither adds read scalability.
x.C: Adding reader instances scales read capacity, and RDS Proxy pools connections and speeds failover, so the application handles more load with less downtime during failover.
x.D: A DMS replication into Redis with write-around adds complexity and doesn't scale writes.

x.A: A Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint with a rule forwards DNS queries from the VPC to the on-premises DNS servers over the VPN, so the application can resolve private on-premises names securely.
x.B: An inbound endpoint lets on-premises resolvers query Route 53 for VPC names, which is the opposite direction.
x.C: A private hosted zone holds records for names in AWS, and doesn't resolve on-premises names.
x.D: A public hosted zone exposes DNS records to the internet, which isn't secure for private services.

x.A: DynamoDB has a 400 KB item limit, so it can't store photos up to 20 MB, and it's costly for large objects.
x.B: Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves photos between tiers as their access changes, with no retrieval fees, which suits photos with mixed viewing patterns. DynamoDB stores the metadata and the S3 locations for fast lookup.
x.C: Moving every photo to Standard-IA after 30 days adds retrieval fees for photos that are still heavily viewed, and object tags aren't good for searching metadata.
x.D: Glacier isn't suitable for photos that users view on demand, because retrieval takes time, and OpenSearch costs more for metadata.

x.A: Round robin sends requests evenly regardless of how busy each target is, so overloaded instances still get new requests. ActiveConnectionCount is also a load balancer level metric, not a per-target measure.
x.B: Least outstanding requests is the right algorithm, but ActiveConnectionCount is a load-balancer-level metric, so it doesn't show which individual targets are overloaded. This option pairs it with the wrong metrics.
x.C: Round robin doesn't take the load on each instance into account.
x.D: The ALB's least outstanding requests algorithm routes new requests to targets with the fewest pending requests, so overloaded instances don't get new ones. The metrics RequestCount and TargetResponseTime show the load.

x.A: A Budgets Savings Plans coverage budget works, but it's configured per budget and isn't the simplest way to get an alert when coverage drops.
x.B: A Lambda function and SES for coverage reports means writing and running custom code.
x.C: A Budgets report only sends scheduled reports, not alerts when coverage drops.
x.D: A Savings Plans alert subscription with all notification options emails you when coverage or utilization changes, which is the simplest and most efficient setup.

x.A: MSK can be made publicly accessible, and with mutual TLS authentication, data in transit is encrypted. Making the existing cluster publicly accessible takes the least change.
x.B: Creating a new VPC and a new cluster means building more infrastructure and migrating, which is more work.
x.C: An ALB can't front a Kafka cluster, because Kafka uses TCP and the ALB works with HTTP and HTTPS.
x.D: An NLB in private subnets isn't publicly reachable, and Kafka doesn't use HTTPS listeners.

x.A: An internet-facing Transfer Family server exposes the SFTP endpoint to the internet, which isn't needed because the company already has connectivity to the on-premises network.
x.B: A single-AZ, internet-facing server isn't resilient and also exposes the endpoint to the internet.
x.C: Periodic checking with Step Functions doesn't process orders immediately and adds complexity.
x.D: An internal Transfer Family SFTP server across two AZs is secure and resilient, files land in S3, and a managed workflow invokes the Lambda function as soon as a file is uploaded, so orders are processed immediately.

x.A: Using EMR on AWS to process the on-premises HDFS data over a VPN moves the processing to the cloud, which the company wants to keep on premises.
x.B: DataSync to copy the data to AWS and EMR to process it moves the processing to the cloud as well.
x.C: EMR on AWS Outposts runs managed Hadoop and Spark on premises, so the data processing stays on premises while the infrastructure becomes scalable and easier to manage.
x.D: Moving the data to S3 with Snowball and processing in EMR in the cloud takes the processing off premises.

x.A: EFS supports NFS only, and Windows instances need SMB, so it can't serve all three operating systems.
x.B: FSx for NetApp ONTAP supports both SMB and NFS for Windows, Mac, and Linux, and auto tiering moves infrequently accessed data to cheaper capacity pool storage with no effort.
x.C: S3 File Gateway runs on premises and adds a gateway to manage, and it isn't what EC2 instances in the Region would use for SMB and NFS.
x.D: FSx for OpenZFS supports NFS only, so Windows instances couldn't use SMB.

x.A: Running the application as a single Lambda function keeps it a monolith, and Lambda's 15 minute limit is shorter than the 20 minute report.
x.B: Spot Instances can be interrupted, and reports must restart from the beginning after an interruption, so they're a poor choice.
x.C: Microservices on ECS with service auto scaling make the application flexible and scalable, so modules can be updated gradually. Rolling deployments limit downtime during patches.
x.D: A single Beanstalk environment with all-at-once deployment keeps the monolith and causes downtime on each deployment.

x.A: Spot Fleet with EC2 instances means managing servers, and Spot Instances can be interrupted, so it isn't serverless.
x.B: Elastic Beanstalk manages the environment, but it still runs on servers, so it isn't serverless and it has more infrastructure.
x.C: EKS with self-managed instances has a lot of infrastructure and operational work.
x.D: Lambda supports Python, scales automatically to hundreds of requests per second, and needs no infrastructure or operational support.

x.A: A transit gateway with a transit VIF to the Direct Connect connection and route propagation lets all 30 VPCs and the on-premises network communicate through one central hub, with the least administration.
x.B: Direct Connect gateways need a virtual private gateway for each VPC, and VPCs can't talk to each other through it, so it takes more work.
x.C: A transit VPC with peering connections is complex, and peering isn't transitive, so it needs many connections and route updates.
x.D: 30 separate VPN connections is a lot to manage and doesn't use the Direct Connect link.

x.A: You can't attach a second role to an EC2 instance. An instance has a single IAM role through its instance profile.
x.B: Systems Manager uses an instance profile role for managed instances, not an IAM user.
x.C: Default Host Configuration Management lets Systems Manager manage EC2 instances without attaching an instance profile or changing the existing role, so running applications aren't disrupted.
x.D: Removing the existing policies from the role would break the instances' access to the RDS databases.

x.A: Scaling nodes by memory usage still needs something to do the scaling, and it doesn't address adding nodes when pods can't be scheduled.
x.B: The Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes when pods can't be scheduled because the cluster is full, and removes them when they're not needed, so the cluster scales with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler.
x.C: A Lambda function to resize the cluster is custom code to build and maintain.
x.D: An EC2 Auto Scaling group by itself doesn't know about pending pods, so it doesn't scale nodes based on Kubernetes demand.

x.A: Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers but doesn't affect storage costs, and it adds charges.
x.B: Frequently replacing large objects with multipart uploads can leave incomplete parts that are stored and billed. A lifecycle policy that deletes incomplete multipart uploads removes those hidden costs.
x.C: S3 Inventory lists objects and doesn't control archival or reduce storage cost.
x.D: CloudFront caches content at edge locations, and it doesn't reduce the number of objects stored in S3.
